notes.b: The location of a home is decided by the site's suitability, the household's needs and the cost of the site.
points: Urban or rural setting: urban sites offer shops, transport and services, while rural sites offer space but may need a private water supply and waste treatment.
Proximity to family, work, schools and shops affects daily travel time and the ease of family life.
Ground conditions: a stable soil structure and freedom from flood risk are checked by a site survey before building.
Aspect: the orientation of the site determines how much daylight and solar heat the house receives.
Budget: the price of the site and the cost of connecting services limit the location a household can afford.
Building and planning regulations that apply to the area can restrict where and how a house may be built.
Setting: a case study of a family with particular needs, used to choose the location, house design, interior and services for that family.
House style is chosen by comparing traditional and modern designs, and bungalow and two-storey layouts, against the family's budget.
Size, age group and lifestyle of the family determine the number of bedrooms, the amount of living space and the need for storage.
Special needs, such as a wheelchair user, may require a single-storey house, step-free access and wider doors.
Potential to convert the attic, extend the house or add a garage must be checked against planning rules for the area.
Personal taste and the style of neighbouring houses determine whether a design fits its surroundings.
Planning permission from the local authority is required for most building work unless the development is exempt under the planning regulations.
Outline permission establishes whether the planning authority agrees in principle to a development, before detailed plans are prepared.
An outline application needs only a site map showing the location and layout of the proposed house, not detailed house plans.
Full permission requires detailed plans and drawings, the site layout, details of water supply and drainage, and the materials to be used in construction.
Full permission also requires the appropriate fee, copies of the public notices and the position of the site notice.
1. Publish a notice of intention to apply in a local newspaper, and erect a site notice on the proposed site.
2. Lodge the application, the site maps, the house plans and the fee with the local authority, which acknowledges receipt.
3. The application is placed on the planning register, where members of the public can inspect it and lodge written objections.
4. Planning officials inspect the site before a decision is made.
5. The authority grants or refuses permission; if permission is refused, the applicant must be given the reasons.
6. Appeals against the decision of the planning authority are made to An Coimisiún Pleanála, which replaced An Bord Pleanála in June 2025.
Diagram: a flowchart of the six stages of full planning permission, from the notices through to the decision and the appeal route.
Developments must fit in with the local development plan for the area.
Houses must not be built so that they overlook neighbours.
Industrial factories must not be built in residential areas.
Scenic areas have restrictions on house building, and new houses must conform to the style of others in the area.
Architect: advises on the site and design, prepares the plans and drawings, applies for planning permission and may supervise construction.
Engineer: advises on the structure, supervises structural work and solves building problems.
Surveyor: surveys the site and building, identifies potential problem areas and recommends how to deal with them before they affect the building.
Solicitor: handles the legal side, including contracts, title deeds, rights of way checked with the Land Registry, and legal advice on building and planning regulations.
Builder: agrees the price and completion date, prepares the site, manages subcontractors such as electricians and plumbers, and rectifies faults.
Other services include interior designers, landscape architects, electricians, plumbers and BER assessors.
A book of house plans offers pre-drawn designs at lower cost, but the plans still need planning permission and may need an architect or engineer to adapt them to the site.

keyTerms.definition: Approval from the local authority that is required before most house building or extension work may begin.
A preliminary approval, based on a site map, which shows whether the planning authority agrees in principle to a development.
Approval given on detailed plans, drawings and specifications, after public notice and consideration of objections.
A notice displayed on the proposed site to inform the public that a planning application has been made.
The public record kept by the local authority of planning applications, which members of the public may inspect.
The direction a site or house faces, which determines the daylight and solar heat it receives.
A professional who surveys a site or building, identifies problems and recommends solutions.
Documents proving legal ownership of a property, checked by a solicitor during a purchase.
The builder's final rectification of faults and unfinished work before a house is handed over.
A set of pre-drawn house designs that a buyer can purchase at lower cost than an architect's design.

factCards.term: What an outline application must include
factCards.definition: A site map showing the location and layout of the proposed house, without detailed house plans.

factCards.term: Four details a full application must contain
factCards.definition: Detailed plans with elevations and finishes; site layout with water supply and drainage; copies of the public notices; the fee and details of materials.

factCards.term: Three reasons a house needs approval before building
factCards.definition: To make sure houses fit the local development plan; to stop houses overlooking neighbours; to keep factories out of residential areas.

factCards.term: Body that hears appeals against a planning decision
factCards.definition: An Coimisiún Pleanála, which replaced An Bord Pleanála in June 2025.

factCards.term: Role of the site and building survey professional
factCards.definition: To survey the site and building, identify problem areas and recommend solutions before they affect the structure.

factCards.term: Three tasks of a solicitor in a house purchase
factCards.definition: Checking the title deeds; checking rights of way with the Land Registry; advising on building and planning regulations.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between outline planning permission and full planning permission.
questions.model: Outline permission establishes whether the planning authority agrees in principle to the development. It needs only a site map showing the location and layout, not detailed house plans. Full permission needs detailed plans and drawings, site layout with water supply and drainage details, the fee, copies of the public notices and the materials to be used. Full permission is the decision that allows building to begin.

questions.prompt: Discuss the professional services a family would use when building a new house, and explain the role each one plays.
questions.model: Architect: advises on site and design, prepares plans and drawings, applies for planning permission and may oversee construction. Engineer: advises on the structure, supervises structural work and solves building problems. Surveyor: surveys the site and building, identifies problem areas and recommends solutions. Solicitor: handles contracts, title deeds, rights of way and legal advice on building and planning regulations. Builder: agrees price and timescale, prepares the site, manages subcontractors and rectifies faults. Other services include interior designers, electricians, plumbers and BER assessors. Each professional should be linked to the stage at which they are needed, and the answer should explain how the services work together to produce a house that meets planning and building standards.
